                                           PROJECT NO. 58482

LARGE LOAD DEMAND                              §            PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
MANAGEMENT SERVICE                             §                     OF TEXAS
                                               §
                                               §


 EOLIAN, L.P.’S COMMENTS TO COMMISSION STAFF’S MARCH 23, 2026 MEMO AND
                        QUESTIONS FOR COMMENT


       Eolian, L.P. (“Eolian”) files these comments in response to Public Utility Commission of Texas
(Commission) Staff’s request for feedback on two options being considered for implementing Section
39.170(b) of the Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) relating to the creation of a Large Load
Demand Management Service, and request for comments on questions to help formulate a draft
proposed rule to implement PURA §39.170(b) and establish a framework for the Large Load Demand
Management Program.1

                                      I.      INTRODUCTION

       Eolian is a Corporate Member of the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc. (“ERCOT”)
and participates in the ERCOT market through the ownership and operation of energy assets and
infrastructure within the region. Eolian is also engaged in the development of integrated projects
involving generation, energy storage, and large electrical loads, including facilities supporting critical
industrial and manufacturing operations. Eolian appreciates the opportunity to comment in this
proceeding.

       PURA § 39.170(b), as enacted by Senate Bill (“SB”) 6, directs the Commission to require
ERCOT to develop a reliability service to procure demand reductions from large load customers for
deployment during anticipated emergency conditions. The statute further requires that the
Commission’s rules define deployment during extreme weather events, establish advance notice and
performance requirements, and prohibit participation based on wholesale price responsiveness or
overlapping service obligations.

       As reflected in the attached comments, implementation of PURA § 39.170(b) requires clear
delineation between this voluntary service and the mandatory curtailment framework under PURA §
39.170(a). Absent such clarity, the rule risks creating ambiguity in deployment, inconsistent

       1
        Staff’s Memo and Questions for Comment w/April 8 Deadline, Project No. 58482, Large Load Demand
Management Service (March 23, 2026).
                                                        1
 obligations, and operational inefficiencies. These comments therefore focus on preserving statutory
distinctions and sequencing, establishing objective and bounded deployment criteria, aligning
obligations with demonstrated capability, and ensuring a procurement framework that supports
reliable, dispatchable performance.

                                    II.     GENERAL COMMENTS

A.      Need for Clarification

        In developing the draft rule, Commission Staff should address the material risk of operational
and regulatory misalignment between PURA §§ 39.170(a) and 39.170(b). These provisions establish
two distinct, but related, curtailment mechanisms within ERCOT’s reliability framework, each
triggered under different system conditions and serving different functional roles. Absent clear
delineation, the rule risks creating ambiguity in deployment, inconsistent obligations for large loads,
and operational inefficiencies during system stress events.

B.      Distinct Statutory Functions: Capability vs. Service

        PURA § 39.170(a) and § 39.170(b) serve fundamentally different statutory functions.
Subsection (a) establishes a non-market, infrastructure-based reliability backstop by requiring
transmission providers, under ERCOT oversight, to ensure that certain large loads are physically and
operationally capable of curtailment during firm load shed. By contrast, subsection (b) directs ERCOT
to procure demand reductions through a competitive, market-based reliability service, subject to
defined eligibility criteria, participation restrictions, and compensation. Read together, these provisions
reflect a layered, forward-looking framework in which subsection (a) embeds baseline curtailment
capability within interconnection and operations, while subsection (b) monetizes voluntary
participation in a structured reliability service.

C.      Triggering Conditions and Implied Sequencing

The statutory provisions are also distinguished by their triggering conditions. Subsection (a) applies
“during firm load shed,” corresponding to involuntary, last-resort emergency actions, while subsection
(b) applies in anticipation of emergency conditions and during extreme weather events, reflecting a
pre-contingency or early-stage reliability tool. This distinction implies a sequencing framework in
which subsection (b) is intended to mitigate system stress before conditions escalate to the point where
subsection (a) must be invoked. The Commission’s rule should be designed to preserve this sequencing
and avoid operational overlap.

                                                        2
 D.      Overlapping Applicability to Large Loads

        Both provisions apply to the same class of customers—large loads—and may operate on the
same underlying demand. Subsection (a) imposes a mandatory capability requirement on certain newly
interconnected loads, while subsection (b) establishes a voluntary, compensated participation construct
that is not limited by interconnection date but includes participation restrictions, including limitations
on price responsiveness and participation in other reliability or ancillary services. The statute does not
explicitly address how these regimes interact when applied to the same load, creating a risk of
conflicting or duplicative obligations.

E.      Key Areas of Ambiguity Requiring Clarification

        Several areas of potential ambiguity warrant clarification in the rule. Although PURA §
39.170(a) and (b) apply to overlapping classes of large loads, they impose distinct obligations with
different eligibility criteria. Subsection (a) establishes a mandatory curtailment capability applicable to
certain newly interconnected loads, while subsection (b) establishes a voluntary service subject to
participation restrictions, including limitations on price responsiveness and participation in other
services. As a result, a large load may be subject to mandatory curtailment under subsection (a) while
being ineligible to participate in subsection (b), demonstrating that the provisions are not aligned and
operate under distinct eligibility and participation criteria.

        In addition, the statute does not specify how ERCOT should sequence deployment between the
two constructs, including when and how the system transitions from voluntary demand reductions
under subsection (b) to mandatory curtailment under subsection (a). The rule should therefore clarify
that participation in subsection (b) does not modify or expand obligations under subsection (a), and
should establish clear, non-overlapping deployment triggers. Finally, cross-references to PURA §
37.0561(e), particularly as applied to large loads with onsite generation, should be narrowly applied to
avoid introducing requirements beyond those contemplated in PURA § 39.170.

F.      Recommended Clarifications to Preserve Statutory Structure

        To address these issues, the Commission should adopt clarifications that preserve the statutory
distinction between mandatory emergency capability and voluntary reliability service participation,
while ensuring operational feasibility and commercial reasonableness. Specifically, the rule should:

     1. Confirm that PURA § 39.170(a) establishes a baseline emergency curtailment capability
        limited to firm load shed conditions, and that participation under PURA § 39.170(b) is strictly
        voluntary and does not alter obligations under subsection (a);

                                                          3
      2. Clearly delineate triggering conditions and sequencing by aligning subsection (b) with pre-
        emergency conditions (e.g., EEA1 and EEA2) and reserving subsection (a) for firm load shed
        (EEA3), while prohibiting overlapping activation for the same large load;

     3. Ensure that curtailment requirements account for facility-specific operational constraints,
        including ramp-down limitations, minimum operating levels, and safety, environmental, and
        equipment considerations;

     4. Define curtailment and performance metrics in a manner that reflects industrial operations,
        including recognition of partial curtailment and necessary operating load, and limit penalties
        where deviations are attributable to validated operational constraints;

     5. Clarify that ordinary operational practices, including internal load management and
        transmission-related practices, do not constitute disqualifying price responsiveness, and that
        participation does not require withdrawal from unrelated commercial arrangements;

     6. Align compensation and performance obligations with demonstrated capability and operational
        impact, with appropriate limitations on performance risk;

     7. Limit infrastructure requirements under subsection (a) to equipment reasonably necessary to
        support firm load shed capability, ensure appropriate cost allocation, and restrict the use of
        operational data to reliability purposes;

     8. Establish clear lines of operational authority and communication protocols among ERCOT,
        TDSPs, and large loads to prevent conflicting instructions and ensure coordinated deployment;

     9. Clarify the treatment of critical load designations, including that participation under subsection
        (b) does not impair critical load status or restoration priority;

     10. Provide clear transition provisions confirming that pre-existing facilities are not subject to new
         subsection (a) requirements, address the treatment of expansions, and avoid duplicative
         obligations with other interconnection frameworks;

     11. Include appropriate liability protections for non-performance driven by safety, environmental,
         or operational constraints; and

     12. Maintain confidentiality protections for operational and facility-specific data, limiting
         disclosure to what is necessary for validation and settlement.

G.      Conclusion

        Absent these clarifications, the rule risks conflating two distinct statutory constructs, leading to
inconsistent application, reduced participation, and potential operational conflicts during system
emergencies. The Commission should therefore ensure that the final rule provides clear, enforceable
boundaries between subsections (a) and (b), consistent with their respective statutory purposes.




                                                         4
                 III.    RESPONSES TO COMMISSION STAFF’S QUESTIONS

1.     Of the two options described in the attached slides, an as-needed service or a seasonal
       service, which is the better option to implement PURA § 39.170(b) and why?

       A seasonal procurement construct is likely to be more workable from an implementation
standpoint, particularly in light of participation constraints for large loads that are not otherwise price
responsive. While either approach could be made to function, a seasonal structure provides a defined
procurement horizon and clearer operational expectations, which tends to better support participation
decisions for loads with fixed or high-value industrial processes and reduces reliance on discretionary
or ad hoc deployment decisions..
       An as-needed construct, by comparison, introduces a level of uncertainty that may limit
engagement. Where curtailment is not inherently economic, large loads must evaluate participation
based on forward planning, internal approvals, and, in some cases, supporting infrastructure
investments. Absent a predictable procurement cycle or commitment period, there is reduced incentive
to develop or maintain the capabilities necessary to participate and a greater likelihood that the service
is relied upon as a residual or gap-filling tool outside defined parameters.
       A seasonal framework also more closely tracks existing ERCOT reliability service constructs,
which may simplify administration and reduce implementation risk. Although not dispositive, this
alignment provides a more familiar structure for qualification, procurement, and deployment based on
predefined commitments rather than real-time discretion.
       From a resource perspective, participation is more likely to come from large loads that have
invested in on-site dispatchable generation or storage and can provide flexibility without interrupting
core operations. A seasonal construct is better suited to accommodate these configurations by
providing sufficient lead time and operational certainty. An as-needed approach, in contrast, presents a
higher risk of limited participation and may constrain the overall effectiveness of the service while
increasing the risk of inconsistent or discretionary deployment.

2.     PURA § 39.170(b) states the commission must require ERCOT to develop a reliability
       service to be deployed in the event of an anticipated emergency condition. PURA §
       39.170(b)(1) states the rules governing the new service must specify the periods when the
       service may be used to assist with maintaining reliability during extreme weather events.

               a.   Does PURA authorize ERCOT to deploy the new service in circumstances
                    other than extreme weather events? If yes, what kind of events?

       PURA § 39.170(b) does not authorize unrestricted deployment of the new service outside the

                                                         5
 context of extreme weather events. The statute contains limiting language that must be given operative
effect. Subsection (b)(1) requires that Commission rules “must specify the periods when the service
may be used…during extreme weather events,” which functions as a constraint on the scope of
permissible deployment rather than a discretionary guideline. Read together with the reference to
“anticipated emergency condition,” the statute permits deployment only where the underlying
reliability risk is causally and temporally connected to an extreme weather event, rather than across all
Energy Emergency Alerts or generalized system conditions.
        Subsection (b)(2) reinforces this limitation by requiring advance notice and sustained
curtailment, which establish a pre-event, forecastable construct. These features are inconsistent with a
broadly deployable or discretionary real-time reliability tool and instead reflect a targeted mechanism
intended to address identifiable, weather-driven risks before they escalate to firm load shed through
structured, forward commitments rather than operator-discretionary actions.
        Within those constraints, the Commission may implement, through rule-based and objectively
defined criteria, the contours of an “anticipated emergency condition.” That term may reasonably
encompass pre-event reliability risks identified through ERCOT’s forecasting and operational
processes—such as expected reserve margin degradation driven by forecasted extreme temperatures,
correlated outages, fuel limitations, or weather-related transmission constraints—provided that such
conditions are defined ex ante through objective, transparent indicators and where those indicators
demonstrate a credible and proximate risk of escalation absent intervention. In this narrow sense,
deployment may occur in advance of an EEA, but only as a forward-looking, scheduled reliability
measure tied to an impending extreme weather event and not as a discretionary tool for real-time
system balancing or gap-filling.
        That implementation authority is not unbounded. Any interpretation that permits deployment
based on generalized system tightness, economic conditions, or non-weather-related contingencies
would sever the required nexus to extreme weather events and render subsection (b)(1)’s limiting
language ineffective. It would also risk converting the service into an additional out-of-market
reliability mechanism, duplicating or displacing existing market constructs and expanding ERCOT’s
authority beyond the statute in a manner inconsistent with the defined sequencing between subsections
(b) and (a).
        Accordingly, PURA § 39.170(b) authorizes deployment outside the precise timing of an
extreme weather event only to the limited extent necessary to address forecasted, weather-linked
reliability risks in advance of such events. A legally and operationally sound implementation should

                                                       6
 therefore confine deployment to conditions that are (i) identifiable in advance based on objective
system indicators, (ii) temporally proximate to a pending extreme weather event, and (iii) reasonably
likely, absent intervention, to result in an EEA or firm load shed, and should be implemented through
predefined, non-discretionary triggers that preserve the distinction between subsection (b) as a pre-
contingency tool and subsection (a) as a last-resort measure.

               b.   Should the commission define “extreme weather event” and, if so, how should
                    it be defined?

       The Commission should adopt a clear and bounded definition of “extreme weather event” to
give effect to PURA § 39.170(b)(1)’s requirement that the periods of service deployment be specified
and to ensure consistent and predictable application across ERCOT and transmission providers. A
defined standard is necessary to provide regulatory certainty and to prevent expansion of the service
beyond its statutory purpose.
       The definition should be anchored in objective, observable, and verifiable criteria that establish
a direct causal and temporal connection between weather conditions and material system reliability
risk. At a minimum, this should include sustained or forecasted temperature extremes, abnormal or
prolonged weather patterns affecting generation availability or fuel supply, and weather-driven
transmission constraints. The definition should also require that such conditions are reasonably
expected to result in deteriorating system margins or an elevated risk of Energy Emergency Alerts
(“EEAs”) absent intervention.
The definition should not rely on open-ended or discretionary standards. Overly broad or indeterminate
language risks expanding the scope of the service beyond weather-driven conditions and undermining
the limiting function of PURA § 39.170(b)(1). Accordingly, the Commission should establish clear
guardrails that constrain deployment to objectively identifiable, weather-linked conditions within a
defined temporal window and that support consistent, rule-based application rather than case-by-case
determinations.
       Importantly, the definition should not be interpreted to encompass generalized system stress,
price formation outcomes, or non-weather-related contingencies. Maintaining this boundary is
necessary to preserve the statutory distinction between targeted, weather-linked reliability tools and
broader system operations, and to avoid creating an additional mechanism for out-of-market
intervention outside the Legislature’s intended scope or disrupting the sequencing between pre-
contingency and emergency actions.


                                                       7
 3.      PURA § 39.170(b)(3) states the rules governing the new service must prohibit
        participation by any large load customer that curtails in response to the wholesale price of
        electricity, as determined by ERCOT, or that otherwise participates in a different
        reliability or ancillary service. PURA § 37.0561(e)—which allows ERCOT to direct a
        large load customer with onsite backup generation to either curtail its load or deploy its
        backup generation under certain circumstances—states that a large load customer with
        onsite backup generation may participate in a service authorized by PURA § 39.170(b).

        PURA § 39.170(b)(3) requires that participation in the new service be limited to resources that
do not curtail in response to wholesale price signals and that are not simultaneously providing another
reliability or ancillary service. At the same time, PURA § 37.0561(e) expressly contemplates that large
load customers with onsite or co-located generation may be directed to curtail load or deploy that
generation and may participate in a service authorized under PURA § 39.170(b). These provisions
should be read together to preserve participation by configurations capable of delivering reliable,
dispatchable performance while preventing purely economic, price-driven behavior.
        In this context, participation supported by behind-the-meter (“BTM”) or co-located generation
and energy storage does not constitute prohibited price-responsive curtailment where the resource is
responding to ERCOT instructions rather than wholesale price signals. Such configurations provide
controllable, infrastructure-backed capability that can be scheduled and dispatched to meet reliability
needs and sustain performance over the duration of an event.
        Similarly, the prohibition on participation in another reliability or ancillary service should be
applied to prevent overlapping or conflicting obligations, not to exclude resources that are capable of
providing multiple services at different times. The relevant inquiry is whether the resource is
concurrently committed in a manner that would result in double-counting or impair performance.
Where that is not the case, participation should not be precluded.
        The Commission should also clarify how participation is evaluated for netted configurations,
including single-line flow (“SLF”) arrangements and similar constructs. In these configurations, import
and export flows are distinct. Curtailment of net load and export of available on-site generation or
storage output are not mutually exclusive and should not be treated as conflicting forms of
participation. Where system design and interconnection constraints support dispatchable capability,
these configurations can provide measurable and reliable performance consistent with § 39.170(b).
        Accordingly, the Commission should adopt an implementation framework that:
     1. Evaluates price responsiveness based on observable behavior relative to wholesale price
        signals;
     2. Permits participation by resources supported by co-located generation or storage where

                                                       8
        performance is dispatchable and not economically contingent; and
   3. Clarifies that participation is not precluded solely by facility configuration or by the ability to
       export energy, provided that reliability service obligations are clearly defined and not
       duplicative.
               a.     What type of qualification is necessary to show that it may take a large load
                      customer 24 hours to ramp down safely?

       PURA § 39.170(b)(2) requires ERCOT to provide at least 24 hours’ notice prior to deployment,
but it does not require that a participating large load fully curtail within that period or reduce to zero.
The statute establishes a notice requirement, not a uniform performance standard.
       Qualification should therefore reflect facility-specific operational characteristics, including
ramp rates, minimum operating levels, and safety or environmental constraints. A rigid requirement for
full curtailment within a fixed timeframe would be inconsistent with the statute and could exclude
resources capable of providing meaningful, reliable partial reductions.
       Participants should be permitted to qualify based on demonstrated capability, including
documented ramp profiles, defined curtailment ranges, and telemetry sufficient to verify performance.
This approach enables predictable and enforceable participation while accommodating staged or partial
curtailment consistent with real-world operations.

               b.     What specific prohibitions not enumerated in PURA § 39.170(b), if any,
                      should apply to participation in the new service?

No comments at this time.

               c.     Should participation in price responsiveness to transmission scarcity such as
                      four coincident peak (4CP) or a successor methodology preclude participation
                      in the new service?

       Participation in transmission cost management constructs such as four coincident peak (“4CP”)
should not, by itself, preclude participation in the new service. PURA § 39.170(b)(3) applies to
curtailment “in response to the wholesale price of electricity,” and transmission charges are
analytically distinct from wholesale energy prices.
       Accordingly, curtailment undertaken to manage transmission cost exposure does not
necessarily constitute the type of price-responsive behavior targeted by the statute. The Commission
should ensure that implementation does not conflate wholesale price responsiveness with transmission-
related cost management.
       More broadly, the evaluation should focus on whether participation in the new service is

                                                        9
 contingent on wholesale price signals or instead reflects committed, dispatchable capability. Where
performance is driven by ERCOT instruction and supported by controllable resources, participation
should remain eligible.

                d.   Should the commission define “curtailment in response to wholesale price of
                     electricity” and, if so, how should it be defined?

        The Commission should define “curtailment in response to wholesale price of electricity” to
provide clarity and ensure consistent, administrable implementation of PURA § 39.170(b)(3). Absent a
clear definition, there is a risk that the prohibition could be applied too broadly, inadvertently
excluding resources that provide legitimate reliability value.
        A legally supportable definition should focus on causation and intent, and should distinguish
between economically contingent behavior and committed, instruction-based performance.
Specifically, “curtailment in response to wholesale price of electricity” should be defined as a
reduction in load that is primarily motivated by, and contingent upon, contemporaneous or anticipated
wholesale energy price levels, rather than pursuant to a pre-committed obligation or direct ERCOT
instruction.
        The definition should further clarify that curtailment is not considered price-responsive where:
     1. Performance is executed in response to ERCOT deployment instructions under the service;
     2. The resource’s capability is supported by controllable, co-located generation or energy storage
        and is not dependent on wholesale price conditions; or
     3. Load adjustments are undertaken for purposes unrelated to wholesale energy prices, including
        transmission cost management or operational constraints.
Establishing this distinction will ensure that the statutory prohibition is applied consistent with its
purpose—preventing opportunistic, price-driven participation—while preserving eligibility for
resources that provide dispatchable, verifiable reliability capability. A clear, behavior-based definition
will also improve administrability and reduce the risk of inconsistent or overly expansive
interpretations.

4.      How should the target quantity, budget, and price be set for the new service?

        The Commission should adopt a procurement framework that is grounded in clearly defined
reliability objectives and designed to attract resources capable of delivering predictable, controllable,
and sustained performance under the conditions contemplated by PURA § 39.170(b). The framework
should recognize that the service is not intended to elicit discretionary, price-responsive behavior, but

                                                       10
 rather to secure committed capability that can be relied upon during periods of system stress.
Target Quantity
       The target quantity should be established based on a transparent assessment of reliability need
associated with extreme weather conditions, including the level of demand reduction required to
materially reduce the risk of EEAs and firm load shed. This assessment should be forward-looking and
periodically updated to reflect changes in load growth, system conditions, and resource mix.
       In defining the target, priority should be given to resources capable of delivering dispatchable,
controllable, and verifiable performance aligned with the operational needs of the service, including
the ability to respond reliably when called and sustain performance consistent with their demonstrated
capability. The Commission should avoid prescriptive or technology-specific assumptions regarding
duration or performance and instead rely on measured, performance-based qualification criteria. A
quantity-based procurement approach tied to identified reliability risk will better ensure that the service
secures dependable capability and integrates effectively into ERCOT’s broader reliability framework.
Budget
       The Commission should avoid adopting a rigid budget cap that constrains procurement below
the level necessary to achieve the identified reliability objective. A fixed budget risks suppressing
participation and limiting competition, particularly where resources must make operational
commitments or investments to provide reliable performance.
       Instead, the framework should allow total program cost to scale with the quantity of capability
procured, subject to appropriate transparency and oversight. If a budget parameter is used, it should
function as a planning guide rather than a binding constraint that overrides reliability-driven
procurement decisions.
Price Formation
       Pricing should be determined through a competitive procurement process and should be
allowed to clear at levels necessary to attract resources capable of providing firm, dispatchable
performance. The relevant benchmark is not historical wholesale price responsiveness, but the cost of
securing committed capability that can be deployed on instruction and sustained consistent with the
service’s operational requirements, independent of prevailing market prices.
       Resources capable of meeting these requirements may incur costs and operational constraints
that differ materially from discretionary load reductions. Accordingly, compensation should reflect:
   1. The opportunity cost associated with reduced operations or altered operating profiles;
   2. The cost of maintaining and operating controllable capability that enables reliable performance;

                                                        11
        and
   3. The performance risk associated with sustained, non-discretionary obligations.
       An administratively constrained price, or an expectation that participation will emerge at
typical energy price levels, is unlikely to yield sufficient or dependable participation. Allowing prices
to reflect the full cost of delivering reliable capability is necessary to ensure that the service attracts
resources capable of meeting its intended function.
       In addition, the procurement framework should be structured to ensure that all capable resource
configurations are evaluated on a consistent, performance-based basis. Qualification, evaluation, and
selection criteria should be technology-neutral and grounded in objective, verifiable performance
attributes, including response capability, controllability, and ability to sustain delivery consistent with
demonstrated capability. The Commission should avoid procurement constructs that rely on categorical
preferences, administratively imposed proxies, or assumptions that may exclude or devalue otherwise
capable resources.
       To support efficient price discovery and competitive outcomes, the process should provide
transparency into evaluation criteria and ensure that bids are assessed based on comparable
performance metrics. This will help avoid outcomes where capable resources are not fully considered
despite meeting or exceeding the operational requirements of the service, and will promote a level
playing field that aligns compensation with actual reliability value.
Procurement Structure and Implementation Considerations
       To support participation and efficient price discovery, the Commission should consider
procurement structures that provide forward visibility and operational certainty. Seasonal or forward
procurement constructs, in particular, can enable participants to plan operations, commit capability,
and, where applicable, make investments necessary to support reliable performance.
       In addition, qualification and performance requirements should be clearly defined and tied to
measurable capability, with verification frameworks that ensure accountability without imposing
unnecessary complexity. This will help ensure that procured resources can perform as expected while
maintaining a broad and competitive participation pool.
       In sum, the target quantity should be based on defined reliability needs, the budget should not
artificially constrain procurement, and prices should be allowed to reflect the full cost of delivering
dependable, dispatchable capability. A framework that emphasizes forward commitments, controllable
performance, and transparent price formation will better align with the statutory purpose of PURA §
39.170(b) and support the development of resources capable of reliably serving this function.

                                                        12
 5.     What additional information should the Commission consider in its implementation of
       PURA § 39.170(b)?

No comments at this time.

6.     PURA §39.170(a) states: The commission shall require the independent organization
       certified under Section 39.151 for the ERCOT power region to ensure that each electric
       cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, and municipally owned utility serving a
       transmission-voltage customer develops a protocol, including the installation of any
       necessary equipment or technology before the customer is interconnected, to allow the
       load to be curtailed during firm load shed. The electric cooperative, transmission and
       distribution utility, or municipally owned utility shall confer with the customer to the
       extent feasible to shed load in a coordinated manner. This subsection applies only to a
       load interconnected after December 31, 2025, that is not: (1) Load operated by a critical
       load industrial customer, as defined by Section 17.002; or (2) Designated as a critical
       natural gas facility under Section 38.074. Should the Commission include a directive
       implementing PURA §39.170(a)?

       The Commission should not incorporate detailed implementation requirements for PURA §
39.170(a) within this rulemaking. Subsection (a) establishes mandatory interconnection and
operational capability requirements, while subsection (b) creates a voluntary, competitively procured
reliability service. These frameworks serve distinct statutory functions and should be developed
through separate, purpose-built proceedings. Addressing subsection (a) in a standalone process will
allow the Commission to more effectively account for evolving large load architectures,
interconnection configurations, and operational technologies without constraining or distorting the
design of the § 39.170(b) service.
       At a minimum, if the Commission elects to include directive language in this proceeding, it
should be limited to high-level principles that preserve the distinction between mandatory curtailment
capability and voluntary service participation, and that ensure consistent and administrable
coordination between the two constructs.
       In particular, the Commission should clarify that compliance with curtailment obligations—
whether under § 39.170(a) protocols or under deployment of the § 39.170(b) service—should be
evaluated based on net impact to the ERCOT system, rather than the specific internal mechanism by
which that impact is achieved. Where a large load has the capability to offset its grid consumption
through controllable, on-site or co-located resources, performance should be measured as a reduction
in net load at the point of interconnection, regardless of whether that reduction is achieved through
load curtailment, dispatch of on-site generation or storage, or a combination of both. Absent this
clarification, there is a risk that implementation could require simultaneous load curtailment and
deployment of on-site resources, effectively resulting in duplicative performance obligations.
                                                        13
        This issue is particularly important for large domestic industrial and manufacturing facilities,
which often operate continuous or process-critical systems with significant safety, environmental, and
economic constraints. For these facilities, uncoordinated or duplicative curtailment requirements can
result in material operational disruption, equipment damage, or loss of critical production. The
Commission should therefore ensure that implementation of § 39.170(a) appropriately accounts for the
operational characteristics of such loads and does not impose requirements that are impracticable or
inconsistent with safe and reliable operations. This consideration is consistent with the statute’s
recognition of certain critical load categories and supports broader state policy objectives related to
domestic manufacturing, supply chain resilience, and economic development.
       A framework that measures performance based on net system impact, and that allows for the
use of controllable on-site resources to meet curtailment obligations, ensures that these facilities can
contribute to reliability objectives without being forced to cease operations unnecessarily.
       Accordingly, the Commission should either: (i) address § 39.170(a) implementation in a
separate proceeding; or (ii) if addressed here, adopt clear guidance that:
   1. Maintains the distinction between mandatory curtailment capability and voluntary service
       participation;
   2. Evaluates performance based on net load reduction at the point of interconnection;
   3. allows compliance through the use of controllable on-site or co-located resources; and
   4. Avoids duplicative obligations that would require both load curtailment and deployment of
       such resources for the same megawatt obligation.
       This approach preserves alignment between obligation and demonstrated capability, supports
efficient system operations, appropriately accommodates critical industrial and manufacturing loads,
and maintains the investment signal for resources capable of delivering reliable, dispatchable
performance.
                                        IV.     CONCLUSION

       The Commission’s implementation of PURA § 39.170 presents an opportunity to establish a
durable and coherent reliability framework that appropriately balances mandatory emergency
capability with voluntary, market-based participation. As drafted, however, the rule risks conflating
these distinct statutory constructs, creating ambiguity in deployment, misaligned incentives, and
potential operational inefficiencies during system stress events.
       The recommendations set forth in these comments are intended to ensure that PURA §§
39.170(a) and (b) are implemented in a manner that preserves their respective roles, provides clear and

                                                        14
 enforceable boundaries, and supports participation by resources capable of delivering reliable,
dispatchable performance. This includes maintaining strict alignment between statutory triggers and
deployment conditions, avoiding duplicative or impracticable obligations, and ensuring that
procurement and participation frameworks are grounded in objective, performance-based criteria.
       A well-structured implementation will enhance reliability outcomes, support efficient system
operations, and provide the regulatory certainty necessary to encourage continued investment in

       Eolian, L.P. ("Eolian") files these comments in response to Public Utility Commission of Texas
(Commission) Staff's request for feedback on two options being considered for implementing Section
39.170(b) of the Public Utility Regulatory Act ("PtJRA") relating to the creation of a Large Load
Demand Management Service, and request for comments on questions to help formulate a draft
proposed rule to implement PURA §39.170(b) and establish a framework for the Large Load Demand
Management Program.1

                                       I.       INTRODUCTION

       Eolian is a Corporate Member of the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc. ("ERCOT")
and participates in the ERCOT market through the ownership and operation of energy assets and
infrastructure within the region. Eolian is also engaged in the development of integrated projects
involving generation, energy storage, and large electrical loads, including facilities supporting critical
industrial and manufacturing operations. Eolian appreciates the opportunity to comment in this
proceeding.

       PURA § 39.170(b), as enacted by Senate Bill ("SB") 6, directs the Commission to require
ERCOT to develop a reliability service to procure demand reductions from large load customers for
deployment during anticipated emergency conditions.            The statute further requires that the
Commission' s rules define deployment during extreme weather events, establish advance notice and
performance requirements, and prohibit participation based on wholesale price responsiveness or
overlapping service obligations.

       As reflected in the attached comments, implementation of PURA § 39. 170(b) requires clear
delineation between this voluntary service and the mandatory curtailment framework under PURA §
39.170(a). Absent such clarity, the rule risks creating ambiguity in deployment, inconsistent

       1 Staff's Memo and Questions for Comment w/April 8 Deadline, Project No. 58482, Large Load Demand
Management Service (March 23,2026)

 obligations, and operational inefficiencies. These comments therefore focus on preserving statutory
distinctions and sequencing, establishing objective and bounded deployment criteria, aligning
obligations with demonstrated capability, and ensuring a procurement framework that supports
reliable, dispatchable performance.

                                     II.     GENERAL COMMENTS

A.      Need for Clarification

        In developing the draft rule, Commission Staff should address the material risk of operational
and regulatory misalignment between PURA §§ 39. 170(a) and 39.170(b). These provisions establish
two distinct, but related, curtailment mechanisms within ERCOT's reliability framework, each
triggered under different system conditions and serving different functional roles. Absent clear
delineation, the rule risks creating ambiguity in deployment, inconsistent obligations for large loads,
and operational inefficiencies during system stress events.

B.      Distinct Statutory Functions: Capability vs. Service

        PURA § 39.170(a) and § 39.170(b) serve fundamentally different statutory functions.
Subsection (a) establishes a non-market, infrastructure-based reliability backstop by requiring
transmission providers, under ERCOT oversight, to ensure that certain large loads are physically and
operationally capable of curtailment during firm load shed. By contrast, subsection (b) directs ERCOT
to procure demand reductions through a competitive, market-based reliability service, subject to
defined eligibility criteria, participation restrictions, and compensation. Read together, these provisions
reflect a layered, forward-looking framework in which subsection (a) embeds baseline curtailment
capability within interconnection and operations, while subsection (b) monetizes voluntary
participation in a structured reliability service.

C.      Triggering Conditions and Implied Sequencing

The statutory provisions are also distinguished by their triggering conditions. Subsection (a) applies
"during firm load shed," corresponding to involuntary, last-resort emergency actions, while subsection
(b) applies in anticipation of emergency conditions and during extreme weather events, reflecting a
pre-contingency or early-stage reliability tool. This distinction implies a sequencing framework in
which subsection (b) is intended to mitigate system stress before conditions escalate to the point where
subsection (a) must be invoked. The Commission's rule should be designed to preserve this sequencing
and avoid operational overlap.

                                                        2
 D.      Overlapping Applicability to Large Loads

        Both provisions apply to the same class of customers-large loads-and may operate on the
same underlying demand. Subsection (a) imposes a mandatory capability requirement on certain newly
interconnected loads, while subsection (b) establishes a voluntary, compensated participation construct
that is not limited by interconnection date but includes participation restrictions, including limitations
on price responsiveness and participation in other reliability or ancillary services. The statute does not
explicitly address how these regimes interact when applied to the same load, creating a risk of
conflicting or duplicative obligations.

E.      Key Areas of Ambiguity Requiring Clarification

        Several areas of potential ambiguity warrant clarification in the rule. Although PURA §
39.170(a) and (b) apply to overlapping classes of large loads, they impose distinct obligations with
different eligibility criteria. Subsection (a) establishes a mandatory curtailment capability applicable to
certain newly interconnected loads, while subsection (b) establishes a voluntary service subject to
participation restrictions, including limitations on price responsiveness and participation in other
services. As a result, a large load may be subject to mandatory curtailment under subsection (a) while
being ineligible to participate in subsection (b), demonstrating that the provisions are not aligned and
operate under distinct eligibility and participation criteria.

        In addition, the statute does not specify how ERCOT should sequence deployment between the
two constructs, including when and how the system transitions from voluntary demand reductions
under subsection (b) to mandatory curtailment under subsection (a). The rule should therefore clarify
that participation in subsection (b) does not modify or expand obligations under subsection (a), and
should establish clear, non-overlapping deployment triggers. Finally, cross-references to PURA §
37.0561(e), particularly as applied to large loads with onsite generation, should be narrowly applied to
avoid introducing requirements beyond those contemplated in PURA § 39.170.

F.      Recommended Clarifications to Preserve Statutory Structure

        To address these issues, the Commission should adopt clarifications that preserve the statutory
distinction between mandatory emergency capability and voluntary reliability service participation,
while ensuring operational feasibility and commercial reasonableness. Specifically, the rule should:

     1. Confirm that PURA § 39.170(a) establishes a baseline emergency curtailment capability
        limited to firm load shed conditions, and that participation under PURA § 39. 170(b) is strictly
        voluntary and does not alter obligations under subsection (a);

                                                           3
      2. Clearly delineate triggering conditions and sequencing by aligning subsection (b) with pre-
        emergency conditions (e.g., EEA1 and EEA2) and reserving subsection (a) for firm load shed
        (EEA3), while prohibiting overlapping activation for the same large load;

     3. Ensure that curtailment requirements account for facility-specific operational constraints,
        including ramp-down limitations, minimum operating levels, and safety, environmental, and
        equipment considerations;

     4. Define curtailment and performance metrics in a manner that reflects industrial operations,
        including recognition of partial curtailment and necessary operating load, and limit penalties
        where deviations are attributable to validated operational constraints;

     5. Clarify that ordinary operational practices, including internal load management and
        transmission-related practices, do not constitute disqualifying price responsiveness, and that
        participation does not require withdrawal from unrelated commercial arrangements;

     6. Align compensation and performance obligations with demonstrated capability and operational
        impact, with appropriate limitations on performance risk;

     7. Limit infrastructure requirements under subsection (a) to equipment reasonably necessary to
        support firm load shed capability, ensure appropriate cost allocation, and restrict the use of
        operational data to reliability purposes;

     8. Establish clear lines of operational authority and communication protocols among ERCOT,
        TDSPs, and large loads to prevent conflicting instructions and ensure coordinated deployment;

     9. Clarify the treatment of critical load designations, including that participation under subsection
        (b) does not impair critical load status or restoration priority;

     10. Provide clear transition provisions confirming that pre-existing facilities are not subject to new
        subsection (a) requirements, address the treatment of expansions, and avoid duplicative
        obligations with other interconnection frameworks;

     11. Include appropriate liability protections for non-performance driven by safety, environmental,
        or operational constraints; and

     12. Maintain confidentiality protections for operational and facility-specific data, limiting
        disclosure to what is necessary for validation and settlement.

G.      Conclusion

        Absent these clarifications, the rule risks conflating two distinct statutory constructs, leading to
inconsistent application, reduced participation, and potential operational conflicts during system
emergencies. The Commission should therefore ensure that the final rule provides clear, enforceable
boundaries between subsections (a) and (b), consistent with their respective statutory purposes.

                  III.      RESPONSES TO COMMISSION STAFF'S OUESTIONS

1.     Of the two options described in the attached slides, an as-needed service or a seasonal
       service, which is the better option to implement PURA § 39.170(b) and why?

       A seasonal procurement construct is likely to be more workable from an implementation
standpoint, particularly in light of participation constraints for large loads that are not otherwise price
responsive. While either approach could be made to function, a seasonal structure provides a defined
procurement horizon and clearer operational expectations, which tends to better support participation
decisions for loads with fixed or high-value industrial processes and reduces reliance on discretionary
or ad hoc deployment decisions..
       An as-needed construct, by comparison, introduces a level of uncertainty that may limit
engagement. Where curtailment is not inherently economic, large loads must evaluate participation
based on forward planning, internal approvals, and, in some cases, supporting infrastructure
investments. Absent a predictable procurement cycle or commitment period, there is reduced incentive
to develop or maintain the capabilities necessary to participate and a greater likelihood that the service
is relied upon as a residual or gap-filling tool outside defined parameters.
       A seasonal framework also more closely tracks existing ERCOT reliability service constructs,
which may simplify administration and reduce implementation risk. Although not dispositive, this
alignment provides a more familiar structure for qualification, procurement, and deployment based on
predefined commitments rather than real-time discretion.
       From a resource perspective, participation is more likely to come from large loads that have
invested in on-site dispatchable generation or storage and can provide flexibility without interrupting
core operations. A seasonal construct is better suited to accommodate these configurations by
providing sufficient lead time and operational certainty. An as-needed approach, in contrast, presents a
higher risk of limited participation and may constrain the overall effectiveness of the service while
increasing the risk of inconsistent or discretionary deployment.

2.     PURA § 39.170(b) states the commission must require ERCOT to develop a reliability
       service to be deployed in the event of an anticipated emergency condition. PURA §
       39.170(b)(1) states the rules governing the new service must specify the periods when the
       service may be used to assist with maintaining reliability during extreme weather events.

               a.       Does PURA authorize ERCOT to deploy the new service in circumstances
                        other than extreme weather events? If yes, what kind of events?

       PURA § 39. 170(b) does not authorize unrestricted deployment of the new service outside the


                                                         5
 context of extreme weather events. The statute contains limiting language that must be given operative
effect. Subsection (b)(1) requires that Commission rules "must specify the periods when the service
may be used... during extreme weather events," which functions as a constraint on the scope of
permissible deployment rather than a discretionary guideline. Read together with the reference to
"anticipated emergency condition," the statute permits deployment only where the underlying
reliability risk is causally and temporally connected to an extreme weather event, rather than across all
Energy Emergency Alerts or generalized system conditions.
        Subsection (b)(2) reinforces this limitation by requiring advance notice and sustained
curtailment, which establish a pre-event, forecastable construct. These features are inconsistent with a
broadly deployable or discretionary real-time reliability tool and instead reflect a targeted mechanism
intended to address identifiable, weather-driven risks before they escalate to firm load shed through
structured, forward commitments rather than operator-discretionary actions.
        Within those constraints, the Commission may implement, through rule-based and objectively
defined criteria, the contours of an "anticipated emergency condition." That term may reasonably
encompass pre-event reliability risks identified through ERCOT's forecasting and operational
processes-such as expected reserve margin degradation driven by forecasted extreme temperatures,
correlated outages, fuel limitations, or weather-related transmission constraints-provided that such
conditions are defined ex ante through obj ective, transparent indicators and where those indicators
demonstrate a credible and proximate risk of escalation absent intervention. In this narrow sense,
deployment may occur in advance of an EEA, but only as a forward-looking, scheduled reliability
measure tied to an impending extreme weather event and not as a discretionary tool for real-time
system balancing or gap-filling.
        That implementation authority is not unbounded. Any interpretation that permits deployment
based on generalized system tightness, economic conditions, or non-weather-related contingencies
would sever the required nexus to extreme weather events and render subsection (b)(1)' s limiting
language ineffective. It would also risk converting the service into an additional out-of-market
reliability mechanism, duplicating or displacing existing market constructs and expanding ERCOT's
authority beyond the statute in a manner inconsistent with the defined sequencing between subsections
(b) and (a).
        Accordingly, PURA § 39.170(b) authorizes deployment outside the precise timing of an
extreme weather event only to the limited extent necessary to address forecasted, weather-linked
reliability risks in advance of such events. A legally and operationally sound implementation should

                                                       6
 therefore confine deployment to conditions that are (i) identifiable in advance based on obj ective
system indicators, (ii) temporally proximate to a pending extreme weather event, and (iii) reasonably
likely, absent intervention, to result in an EEA or firm load shed, and should be implemented through
predefined, non-discretionary triggers that preserve the distinction between subsection (b) as a pre-
contingency tool and subsection (a) as a last-resort measure.

               b.   Should the commission define "extreme weather event" and, if so, how should
                    it be defined?

       The Commission should adopt a clear and bounded definition of "extreme weather event" to
give effect to PURA § 39.170(b)(1)'s requirement that the periods of service deployment be specified
and to ensure consistent and predictable application across ERCOT and transmission providers. A
defined standard is necessary to provide regulatory certainty and to prevent expansion of the service
beyond its statutory purpose.
       The definition should be anchored in objective, observable, and verifiable criteria that establish
a direct causal and temporal connection between weather conditions and material system reliability
risk. At a minimum, this should include sustained or forecasted temperature extremes, abnormal or
prolonged weather patterns affecting generation availability or fuel supply, and weather-driven
transmission constraints. The definition should also require that such conditions are reasonably
expected to result in deteriorating system margins or an elevated risk of Energy Emergency Alerts
("EEAs") absent intervention.
The definition should not rely on open-ended or discretionary standards. Overly broad or indeterminate
language risks expanding the scope of the service beyond weather-driven conditions and undermining
the limiting function of PURA § 39.170(b)(1). Accordingly, the Commission should establish clear
guardrails that constrain deployment to objectively identifiable, weather-linked conditions within a
defined temporal window and that support consistent, rule-based application rather than case-by-case
determinations.
       Importantly, the definition should not be interpreted to encompass generalized system stress,
price formation outcomes, or non-weather-related contingencies. Maintaining this boundary is
necessary to preserve the statutory distinction between targeted, weather-linked reliability tools and
broader system operations, and to avoid creating an additional mechanism for out-of-market
intervention outside the Legislature's intended scope or disrupting the sequencing between pre-
contingency and emergency actions.

 3.      PURA § 39.170(b)(3) states the rules governing the new service must prohibit
        participation by any large load customer that curtails in response to the wholesale price of
        electricity, as determined by ERCOT, or that otherwise participates in a different
        reliability or ancillary service. PURA § 37.0561(e)-which allows ERCOT to direct a
        large load customer with onsite backup generation to either curtail its load or deploy its
        backup generation under certain circumstances-states that a large load customer with
        onsite backup generation may participate in a service authorized by PURA § 39.170(b).

        PURA § 39.170(b)(3) requires that participation in the new service be limited to resources that
do not curtail in response to wholesale price signals and that are not simultaneously providing another
reliability or ancillary service. At the same time, PURA § 37.0561(e) expressly contemplates that large
load customers with onsite or co-located generation may be directed to curtail load or deploy that
generation and may participate in a service authorized under PURA § 39.170(b). These provisions
should be read together to preserve participation by configurations capable of delivering reliable,
dispatchable performance while preventing purely economic, price-driven behavior.
        In this context, participation supported by behind-the-meter ("BTM') or co-located generation
and energy storage does not constitute prohibited price-responsive curtailment where the resource is
responding to ERCOT instructions rather than wholesale price signals. Such configurations provide
controllable, infrastructure-backed capability that can be scheduled and dispatched to meet reliability
needs and sustain performance over the duration of an event.
        Similarly, the prohibition on participation in another reliability or ancillary service should be
applied to prevent overlapping or conflicting obligations, not to exclude resources that are capable of
providing multiple services at different times. The relevant inquiry is whether the resource is
concurrently committed in a manner that would result in double-counting or impair performance.
Where that is not the case, participation should not be precluded.
        The Commission should also clarify how participation is evaluated for netted configurations,
including single-line flow ("SLF") arrangements and similar constructs. In these configurations, import
and export flows are distinct. Curtailment of net load and export of available on-site generation or
storage output are not mutually exclusive and should not be treated as conflicting forms of
participation. Where system design and interconnection constraints support dispatchable capability,
these configurations can provide measurable and reliable performance consistent with § 39.170(b).
        Accordingly, the Commission should adopt an implementation framework that:
     1. Evaluates price responsiveness based on observable behavior relative to wholesale price
        signals;
     2. Permits participation by resources supported by co-located generation or storage where

                                                        8
        performance is dispatchable and not economically contingent; and
   3. Clarifies that participation is not precluded solely by facility configuration or by the ability to
       export energy, provided that reliability service obligations are clearly defined and not
       duplicative.
               a.     What type of qualification is necessary to show that it may take a large load
                      customer 24 hours to ramp down safely?

       PURA § 39.170(b)(2) requires ERCOT to provide at least 24 hours' notice prior to deployment,
but it does not require that a participating large load fully curtail within that period or reduce to zero.
The statute establishes a notice requirement, not a uniform performance standard.
       Qualification should therefore reflect facility-specific operational characteristics, including
ramp rates, minimum operating levels, and safety or environmental constraints. A rigid requirement for
full curtailment within a fixed timeframe would be inconsistent with the statute and could exclude
resources capable of providing meaningful, reliable partial reductions.
       Participants should be permitted to qualify based on demonstrated capability, including
documented ramp profiles, defined curtailment ranges, and telemetry sufficient to verify performance.
This approach enables predictable and enforceable participation while accommodating staged or partial
curtailment consistent with real-world operations.

               b.     What specific prohibitions not enumerated in PURA § 39.170(b), if any,
                      should apply to participation in the new service?

No comments at this time.

               c.     Should participation in price responsiveness to transmission scarcity such as
                      four coincident peak (4CP) or a successor methodology preclude participation
                      in the new service?

       Participation in transmission cost management constructs such as four coincident peak ("4CP")
should not, by itself, preclude participation in the new service. PURA § 39.170(b)(3) applies to
curtailment "in response to the wholesale price of electricity," and transmission charges are
analytically distinct from wholesale energy prices.
       Accordingly, curtailment undertaken to manage transmission cost exposure does not
necessarily constitute the type of price-responsive behavior targeted by the statute. The Commission
should ensure that implementation does not conflate wholesale price responsiveness with transmission-
related cost management.
       More broadly, the evaluation should focus on whether participation in the new service is

                                                         9
 contingent on wholesale price signals or instead reflects committed, dispatchable capability. Where
performance is driven by ERCOT instruction and supported by controllable resources, participation
should remain eligible.

                   d.   Should the commission define "curtailment in response to wholesale price of
                        electricity" and, if so, how should it be defined?

        The Commission should define "curtailment in response to wholesale price of electricity" to
provide clarity and ensure consistent, administrable implementation of PURA § 39.170(b)(3). Absent a
clear definition, there is a risk that the prohibition could be applied too broadly, inadvertently
excluding resources that provide legitimate reliability value.
        A legally supportable definition should focus on causation and intent, and should distinguish
between    economically       contingent   behavior   and        committed,   instruction-based   performance.
Specifically, "curtailment in response to wholesale price of electricity" should be defined as a
reduction in load that is primarily motivated by, and contingent upon, contemporaneous or anticipated
wholesale energy price levels, rather than pursuant to a pre-committed obligation or direct ERCOT
instruction.
        The definition should further clarify that curtailment is not considered price-responsive where:
     1. Performance is executed in response to ERCOT deployment instructions under the service;
     2. The resource' s capability is supported by controllable, co-located generation or energy storage
        and is not dependent on wholesale price conditions; or
     3. Load adjustments are undertaken for purposes unrelated to wholesale energy prices, including
        transmission cost management or operational constraints.
Establishing this distinction will ensure that the statutory prohibition is applied consistent with its
purpose-preventing opportunistic, price-driven participation-while preserving eligibility for
resources that provide dispatchable, verifiable reliability capability. A clear, behavior-based definition
will also improve administrability and reduce the risk of inconsistent or overly expansive
interpretations.

4.      How should the target quantity, budget, and price be set for the new service?

        The Commission should adopt a procurement framework that is grounded in clearly defined
reliability obj ectives and designed to attract resources capable of delivering predictable, controllable,
and sustained performance under the conditions contemplated by PURA § 39.170(b). The framework
should recognize that the service is not intended to elicit discretionary, price-responsive behavior, but

                                                            10
 rather to secure committed capability that can be relied upon during periods of system stress.
Target Ouantitv
       The target quantity should be established based on a transparent assessment of reliability need
associated with extreme weather conditions, including the level of demand reduction required to
materially reduce the risk of EEAs and firm load shed. This assessment should be forward-looking and
periodically updated to reflect changes in load growth, system conditions, and resource mix.
       In defining the target, priority should be given to resources capable of delivering dispatchable,
controllable, and verifiable performance aligned with the operational needs of the service, including
the ability to respond reliably when called and sustain performance consistent with their demonstrated
capability. The Commission should avoid prescriptive or technology-specific assumptions regarding
duration or performance and instead rely on measured, performance-based qualification criteria. A
quantity-based procurement approach tied to identified reliability risk will better ensure that the service
secures dependable capability and integrates effectively into ERCOT' s broader reliability framework.
Budget
       The Commission should avoid adopting a rigid budget cap that constrains procurement below
the level necessary to achieve the identified reliability objective. A fixed budget risks suppressing
participation and limiting competition, particularly where resources must make operational
commitments or investments to provide reliable performance.
       Instead, the framework should allow total program cost to scale with the quantity of capability
procured, subject to appropriate transparency and oversight. If a budget parameter is used, it should
function as a planning guide rather than a binding constraint that overrides reliability-driven
procurement decisions.
Price Formation
       Pricing should be determined through a competitive procurement process and should be
allowed to clear at levels necessary to attract resources capable of providing firm, dispatchable
performance. The relevant benchmark is not historical wholesale price responsiveness, but the cost of
securing committed capability that can be deployed on instruction and sustained consistent with the
service' s operational requirements, independent of prevailing market prices.
       Resources capable of meeting these requirements may incur costs and operational constraints
that differ materially from discretionary load reductions. Accordingly, compensation should reflect:
    1. The opportunity cost associated with reduced operations or altered operating profiles;
   2. The cost of maintaining and operating controllable capability that enables reliable performance;


                                                        11
        and
   3. The performance risk associated with sustained, non-discretionary obligations.
       An administratively constrained price, or an expectation that participation will emerge at
typical energy price levels, is unlikely to yield sufficient or dependable participation. Allowing prices
to reflect the full cost of delivering reliable capability is necessary to ensure that the service attracts
resources capable of meeting its intended function.
       In addition, the procurement framework should be structured to ensure that all capable resource
configurations are evaluated on a consistent, performance-based basis. Qualification, evaluation, and
selection criteria should be technology-neutral and grounded in obj ective, verifiable performance
attributes, including response capability, controllability, and ability to sustain delivery consistent with
demonstrated capability. The Commission should avoid procurement constructs that rely on categorical
preferences, administratively imposed proxies, or assumptions that may exclude or devalue otherwise
capable resources.
       To support efficient price discovery and competitive outcomes, the process should provide
transparency into evaluation criteria and ensure that bids are assessed based on comparable
performance metrics. This will help avoid outcomes where capable resources are not fully considered
despite meeting or exceeding the operational requirements of the service, and will promote a level
playing field that aligns compensation with actual reliability value.
Procurement Structure and Implementation Considerations
       To support participation and efficient price discovery, the Commission should consider
procurement structures that provide forward visibility and operational certainty. Seasonal or forward
procurement constructs, in particular, can enable participants to plan operations, commit capability,
and, where applicable, make investments necessary to support reliable performance.
       In addition, qualification and performance requirements should be clearly defined and tied to
measurable capability, with verification frameworks that ensure accountability without imposing
unnecessary complexity. This will help ensure that procured resources can perform as expected while
maintaining a broad and competitive participation pool.
       In sum, the target quantity should be based on defined reliability needs, the budget should not
artificially constrain procurement, and prices should be allowed to reflect the full cost of delivering
dependable, dispatchable capability. A framework that emphasizes forward commitments, controllable
performance, and transparent price formation will better align with the statutory purpose of PURA §
39.170(b) and support the development of resources capable of reliably serving this function.
